terms.gloss: a tossing, a shaking: of a ship at sea; here, of a plane in turbulence
evidence: Cic. Mur. 4: prope jam ex magnā jactātiōne terram videntem
Curt. 6.5.1: jactātiōnem vulnerum haud facile tolerantem, the jolting (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The classical word for the tossing of a ship in a storm, and so for the bumps of a plane; its use of an aircraft is modern, and ours. No reference work has a word for turbulence; turbulentia is Tertullian’s, and means trouble, disquiet (Lewis & Short). With a child the verb is commoner: āëroplanum jactātur.

terms.gloss: in the passive, be tossed about (of a ship; here, of a plane)
evidence: Verg. A. 1.3: terrīs jactātus et altō (Lewis & Short)

terms.comment: Late, and never of the air: Lewis & Short’s only senses are mental and moral. Use jactātiō.

phrases.latin: Āëroplanum paulum jactātur; nihil est quod timeās.
phrases.english: The plane is bumping a little; there’s nothing to be afraid of.
Fasten your seatbelt: it’s going to be a bit bumpy soon.

phrases.latin: prope jam ex magnā jactātiōne terram videntem
phrases.english: now almost in sight of land after a great tossing

sources: Lewis & Short: jactatio · Lewis & Short: jacto · Lewis & Short: turbulentia
